title: Nearly every piano is slightly out of tune, on purpose
body: Pure musical intervals come from simple frequency ratios: an octave is 2:1 and a perfect fifth is 3:2. The problem is that stacking twelve pure fifths overshoots seven octaves by about a quarter of a semitone, so no keyboard can be pure in every key. Equal temperament instead splits the octave into twelve identical steps, making every interval except the octave slightly impure but letting music sound equally good in all keys.

slides.heading: The maths
slides.text: Each semitone multiplies the frequency by the twelfth root of 2, about 1.0595. Twelve of those steps multiply it by exactly 2: one octave.

slides.heading: What you give up
slides.text: Equal-tempered fifths are only about 2 cents (hundredths of a semitone) narrow, but major thirds are about 14 cents wide, a faint beating trained ears can hear.

slides.heading: Before it took over
slides.text: Older systems such as meantone made common keys sweeter but remote keys harsh. Equal temperament gradually became the Western norm in the 19th century.

slides.question: Which interval stays perfectly pure in equal temperament?
slides.explanation: Twelve equal semitones multiply the frequency by exactly 2, so octaves are pure. Fifths end up about 2 cents narrow and major thirds about 14 cents wide.
